Chapter 6: The Politics of Respectability and the Rise of the “Redneck”
By the late twentieth century, class lines hadn’t vanished—they just found new ways to show up. The words people used to talk about “white trash” kept changing, sometimes softening, sometimes cutting even deeper, but always drawing lines about who belonged and who didn’t.
Down South, a new figure started to stand out: the “redneck.” For some, it was a source of pride. For others, it became a punchline. Picture this—someone in a faded ball cap, sun on his face at a county fair, swapping stories with friends. He’s proud of his roots, but he knows the rest of the world sees him differently. The word “redneck” gets tossed around on TV and in music. Sometimes it feels like a badge of honor, other times, like an insult. He might shrug it off, but let’s be honest—that sting never really goes away.
The whole idea of respectability—who gets seen as decent, or “worthy”—became a powerful force. Politicians and experts talked a lot about the “working class,” but rarely bothered to listen to folks living that reality. The media painted rural and poor whites as either salt-of-the-earth heroes or as backward, even dangerous people. Most of us never stopped to think how those stories shape the way we see our neighbors, and even ourselves.
During the 1970s and 80s, as factories closed and jobs vanished, the old promise of moving up in the world just faded for a lot of people. Towns that once buzzed with manufacturing or mining felt abandoned—their main streets grew quiet, schools struggled, and hope felt scarce. Those who stayed were often blamed for their struggles, told they just needed to work harder, or maybe just leave. The myth that America was a classless society still lingered, but in these places, it rang hollow.
You could hear these changes in music, in comedy, and on TV. Country songs started telling stories of both pride and pain—about holding on to dignity when so much was lost. Sitcoms and stand-up routines made jokes about “rednecks” and “hillbillies.” Sometimes it felt loving, sometimes it stung. The line between laughing with someone and laughing at them? It was razor thin, and people felt it.
The politics of that era leaned hard on class differences. Debates about welfare, crime, and education were often set up to blame the poor for their own troubles. Stereotypes like the “welfare queen” or the “lazy redneck” became shortcuts for big anxieties about change, race, and belonging. Most folks didn’t see how these images were used to justify policies that made life even tougher for those already struggling.
Through it all, the shame and stigma of being poor and white stuck around. Families tried to hide what they were going through, hoping to blend in as middle class, even when the bills kept piling up. That dream of respectability always seemed just out of reach, and chasing it came with a steep price.
